sections.title: Atoms, molecules, valency and radicals; relative masses and the atomic mass unit
Chemical equations, empirical and molecular formulae, percentage composition

summary: 1 u = 1/12 of the mass of a ¹²C atom = 1.66 × 10⁻²⁴ g; relative atomic and molecular masses are unitless ratios; the tabulated atomic mass is an isotope-weighted average.
Formulae come from valencies by criss-cross; learn the radicals with their charges, and remember Hg₂²⁺ (Hg₂Cl₂), S₂O₃²⁻ and Cr₂O₇²⁻.
Percentage of an element = (atoms × A_r)/M × 100; urea is 46.7 % N, CuSO₄·5H₂O is 36.1 % water.
Empirical formula: % → ÷ A_r → ÷ smallest → whole numbers; molecular formula = n × empirical formula, with M = 2 × VD.
Lavoisier (mass), Proust (definite), Dalton (multiple), Richter (reciprocal), Gay-Lussac (gas volumes), Avogadro (equal volumes, equal molecules).
Dalton's indivisibility and identical-mass postulates failed (subatomic particles, isotopes, isobars); conservation of atoms in chemical change survives.
One mole = 6.022 × 10²³ entities (exact since 2019) = M grams = 22.4 L of gas at STP; n = m/M = N/NA = V/22.4.
Limiting reactant = smallest moles ÷ coefficient; it fixes the product. % yield = actual/theoretical × 100.
terms: Atomic mass unit and relative atomic mass

sections.title: Rutherford's and Bohr's atomic models; the spectrum of hydrogen
de Broglie's equation and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle
Orbitals and quantum numbers; Aufbau, Pauli and Hund; electronic configuration

summary: Rutherford: most of the atom is empty; positive charge and mass sit in a nucleus about 10⁻¹⁵ m across. The model fails on stability and on line spectra.
Bohr: stationary orbits with mvr = nh/2π; photons only on jumps, Δ E = hν. For one-electron species r ∝ n^2/Z, v ∝ Z/n, E = -13.6 Z^2/n^2 eV.
Hydrogen lines obey 1/λ = RH(1/n1^2 - 1/n2^2): Lyman (UV), Balmer (visible), Paschen, Brackett, Pfund (IR). A sample falling from level n gives n(n-1)/2 lines.
de Broglie: λ = h/mv; significant only for tiny masses; 2π r = nλ gives Bohr's rule.
Heisenberg: Δ x·Δ p ≥ h/4π, so orbits give way to orbitals (probability regions).
Quantum numbers n, l (0 to n − 1), m (−l to +l), s (±½); radial nodes n − l − 1, angular nodes l.
Aufbau by (n + l), Pauli (two electrons per orbital, opposite spins), Hund (no pairing until each degenerate orbital has one). Cr 3d⁵ 4s¹ and Cu 3d¹⁰ 4s¹; ions lose 4s before 3d.

sections.title: Modern periodic law and table; s, p, d and f blocks; isoelectronic species
Periodic trends: size, ionisation energy, electronegativity, electron affinity and metallic character

summary: Modern periodic law: properties are periodic functions of atomic number; periodicity comes from the recurrence of similar outer configurations.
7 periods (2, 8, 8, 18, 18, 32, 32 elements) and 18 groups; s, p, d and f blocks by the subshell that takes the last electron; He is s-block but sits in group 18.
Group from configuration: s-block ns electrons, p-block 10 + ns + np, d-block ns + (n − 1)d.
Isoelectronic species share an electron count; their radius falls as Z rises.
Across a period Z_eff rises: size falls; IE, EA and electronegativity rise; metallic character and basic character of oxides fall. Down a group the reverse.
IE exceptions Be > B, N > O (Mg > Al, P > S); EA exceptions Cl > F, S > O; noble gases, Be, Mg and N have near-zero or negative EA.
Highest IE He, lowest Cs; most electronegative F (4.0); highest EA Cl. A big jump in successive IEs counts the valence electrons.
Ga < Al in size (poor 3d shielding); Zr ≈ Hf (lanthanoid contraction).

sections.title: Electronic theory of valency; ionic, covalent and coordinate bonds; Lewis structures
VSEPR theory and shapes; valence bond theory, σ and π bonds, hybridisation
Dipole moment, ionic character of covalent bonds and bond length
Hydrogen bonding, metallic bonding and van der Waals forces

summary: Atoms bond to reach a noble-gas configuration: ionic (transfer), covalent (sharing), coordinate (a pair donated by one atom — NH₄⁺, H₃O⁺, H₃N→BF₃). The octet rule fails for BF₃, PCl₅, SF₆, NO and xenon fluorides.
Formal charge = V − L − B/2; the best Lewis structure minimises formal charges.
VSEPR: shape from the steric number SN = ½(V + M − c + a); lp–lp > lp–bp > bp–bp squeezes angles: CH₄ 109.5° > NH₃ 107° > H₂O 104.5°.
Lone pairs in a trigonal bipyramid go equatorial: SF₄ see-saw, ClF₃ T-shaped, XeF₂ linear; XeF₄ is square planar.

σ bonds come from head-on overlap, π bonds from sideways overlap; double = σ + π, triple = σ + 2π. Hybridisation sp, sp², sp³, sp³d, sp³d², sp³d³ for SN 2–7; more s character, shorter and stronger bond.
μ = q × d (debye); symmetric molecules have μ = 0; NH₃ > NF₃; % ionic character = μ(obs)/(e × d) × 100. Fajans: small, highly charged cations and large anions raise covalent character.
Bond length falls as bond order and s character rise; resonance makes equivalent bonds equal.

Hydrogen bonds (F, O, N) explain the high boiling points of H₂O, HF and NH₃, ice floating and o-nitrophenol's volatility; metallic bonds are an electron sea; London forces grow with size and surface area.

sections.title: Classical and electronic concepts of oxidation and reduction; oxidation number
Balancing redox equations by the oxidation-number and ion-electron methods; applications

summary: Classical: oxidation = addition of O or an electronegative element, removal of H or an electropositive element; reduction the reverse.
Electronic: oxidation = loss of electrons, reduction = gain; the oxidant is reduced and the reductant oxidised; both always occur together.
Oxidation number rules: free element 0; F −1; O −2 except peroxides (−1), superoxides (−½) and OF₂ (+2); H +1 except metal hydrides (−1); the sum equals the charge.
Watch the traps: Fe₃O₄ +8/3, S₄O₆²⁻ +2.5, CrO₅ and H₂S₂O₈ +6 (peroxide links), OsO₄ +8, NH₄NO₃ −3 and +5.
Highest oxidation state → only an oxidant; lowest → only a reductant; intermediate → both, and able to disproportionate (H₂O₂, Cl₂ in alkali, Cu⁺, HNO₂).
Balancing: equalise the total change in oxidation number, or add half-reactions after balancing O with H₂O, H with H⁺ (OH⁻ in base) and charge with electrons.
n-factors: MnO₄⁻ 5 (acid), 3 (neutral), 1 (strong base); Cr₂O₇²⁻ 6; moles react in the inverse ratio of n-factors.

summary: Kinetic theory: random elastic motion, no attractions, negligible molecular volume; KE = (3/2)RT per mole for every gas; urms = √3RT/M and ump : uav : urms = 1 : 1.128 : 1.224.
Boyle, Charles, pressure and Avogadro laws combine into PV = nRT (R = 8.314 J or 0.0821 L atm mol⁻¹ K⁻¹); always use kelvin.
Dalton: pi = xiP; Graham: rate ∝ 1/√M (lighter gases diffuse faster; time ∝ √M).
Real gases: Z = PV/nRT; van der Waals a (attraction) and b (excluded volume); ideal behaviour at low P and high T; large a means easy liquefaction.
Vapour pressure depends only on the liquid and T; boiling occurs when VP = external pressure. Surface tension (N m⁻¹) and liquid viscosity (Pa s) fall as T rises.
Liquid crystals (nematic, smectic, cholesteric) flow but keep orientational order; used in LCDs and thermometers. Solubility curves show crystallisation yields; KNO₃ rises steeply, NaCl barely.
Crystalline solids: long-range order, sharp mp, anisotropic; amorphous: short-range order, soften over a range, isotropic. Efflorescent loses water; deliquescent dissolves; hygroscopic absorbs.
7 crystal systems, 14 Bravais lattices; sc, bcc, fcc have Z = 1, 2, 4 and CN 6, 8, 12; ρ = ZM/(a³N_A). Solids are ionic, covalent network, molecular or metallic.
